description:
Redwood Inference is standing up an enterprise-friendly Long Term Support (LTS) channel for the serving runtime, focused on kernel + scheduling stability, predictable patch cadence, and slower-change release notes. The goal is to support Dedicated and Private customers who need a stable runtime baseline for 6–12+ months, with a clear backport policy (security + critical fixes), reproducible builds, and auditable release artifacts.

Goals:
- Establish a Runtime LTS branch strategy (e.g., runtime-1.18-lts) with defined support window and patch cadence (e.g., monthly patches + out-of-band security fixes).
- Publish an explicit backport policy: eligibility criteria, risk rubric, required test/perf gates, and approval workflow.
- Produce enterprise-grade “slower-change” release notes: categorized changes, known issues, upgrade notes, and compatibility matrix.
- Implement tooling: release automation, cherry-pick/backport helpers, CI/perf regression gates, artifact signing/checksums, and version pinning support for Private installer + Helm.
- Define operational ownership: on-call/escalation expectations for LTS, how incidents drive backports, and how to communicate patch availability to Support/CS/Sales.

Non-goals:
- Creating a separate forked runtime architecture; LTS should remain close to mainline with controlled backports.
- Guaranteeing feature parity with main; LTS prioritizes stability over new features.

Primary stakeholders:
- Engineering: Connor O’Brien (Release Eng lead), Mateo Alvarez (VP Eng Runtime), Hiro Tanaka (Kernels), Sofia Ivanova (Scheduling), Noah Patel (runtime architecture), Sahana Iyer (CI/build).
- SRE/Infra: Sean Gallagher, Rafael Mendes, Allison Grant (observability/perf regression signals).
- Product: Marissa Cole, Paula Mendes (release visibility / rollout tooling expectations).
- Customer-facing: Jasmine Liu, Dev Patel (Support), Rachel Kim (Enterprise CS), enterprise AEs (Avery Johnson / Hannah Schmitt) for customer comms.

Constraints and risks:
- Performance regressions are high-severity for enterprise; LTS must enforce perf gates and clear rollback guidance.
- Backports can introduce correctness risk; policy must require minimal diffs, strong test coverage, and explicit approvals.
- Must work across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private packaging; LTS artifacts must be reproducible and traceable to commits.

Execution plan (high level timeline):
- Phase 1 (2–3 weeks): requirements gathering, branch/versioning decision, draft backport rubric, define release note format.
- Phase 2 (4–6 weeks): implement CI + perf gates, automation, packaging/pinning support, draft docs/runbooks.
- Phase 3 (4 weeks): pilot with 1–3 enterprise accounts; cut first LTS patch, validate comms + support workflow.
- Phase 4: GA the LTS channel; publish docs, train Support/CS/Sales, and establish steady-state release cadence and reporting.

files.description: Primary Confluence spec for the LTS initiative: rationale, target customers, support window, branching model, backport eligibility rubric (security/Sev1/Sev2), and approval workflow across Runtime + Release Eng + SRE.
Defines the slower-change release notes template for LTS (categories, performance notes, upgrade notes, known issues, mitigations, CVE format), with examples and required metadata per patch.
Step-by-step runbook for cutting an LTS patch: branch prep, cherry-picks, CI/perf gates, artifact generation/signing, publishing notes, and rollout comms.
Living list of LTS-known issues, affected versions, symptoms, mitigations, and when a fix will be backported vs documented as a workaround.
Performance gating policy for LTS: canonical workloads, acceptable variance thresholds (p50/p95, throughput), GPU SKU coverage, and how results are reviewed before release.
ADR documenting the chosen LTS branching/versioning scheme (e.g., runtime-1.18-lts + patch numbering), how it relates to mainline and customer pinning semantics.
Process doc describing change-control for LTS (required reviewers, risk scoring, release manager responsibilities, exception handling, and how emergency security patches are handled).
Defines SLO expectations for LTS customers (Hosted/Dedicated/Private), escalation paths, and criteria for declaring an LTS patch mandatory vs optional.
Private deployment guidance for adopting LTS: version pinning, upgrade sequencing, rollback procedure, compatibility notes with installer/helm, and validation checklist.
Product-facing launch brief: positioning, customer eligibility, communication plan, and how LTS appears in Console/Docs (what customers will see).
Support/CS playbook: how to handle LTS-related tickets, required data for triage, when to request a backport, and comms templates for patch availability.
Build/CI standards for LTS artifacts: provenance, checksums/signing, SBOM notes, and how to map artifacts to commits and release notes.
Early draft proposal capturing customer pain, proposed support window, expected release cadence, and open questions before ADR approval.
Spreadsheet-style tracker of candidate fixes for the first LTS branch: PR links, risk score, test status, perf impact, approvers, and target patch.
Working notes/checklist used by runtime engineers during the first branch cut, including gotchas and manual steps later moved into a formal runbook.
Draft template for SRE release readiness reviews: monitoring coverage, rollback readiness, load test results, and customer impact assessment.
Product notes on how LTS should be presented in Console (version pinning options, warnings, release note links, and rollout controls).
CSM-facing FAQ draft: what LTS is/isn’t, patch cadence expectations, how to request backports, and how to explain slower-change release notes.
Perf baseline results for the LTS line across representative workloads and GPUs; includes notes on expected variance and known measurement pitfalls.
Slide-style exec update: milestones, risks, staffing needs, pilot accounts, and GA criteria for the LTS channel.
Top-level engineering epic for Runtime LTS branch & release process; contains milestone breakdown, owners, and links to ADR/spec/runbooks.
Ticket to finalize branching/version naming (release/* vs runtime-*-lts), tagging conventions, and compatibility with Private/Helm version pinning.
Engineering work to add labels (backport-candidate, lts-approved) and automation to open backport PRs and track conflicts.
Create CI workflows to test release/* branches with stricter gates, including deterministic build steps and artifact publication staging.
Hook perf-canary results into LTS release gating; define thresholds and required benchmark sets for each patch.
Tooling ticket for generating slower-change release notes from PR labels + curated summaries, including known issues and upgrade notes sections.
Enable Redwood Private installer to pin to a specific runtime LTS patch, verify checksums, and support rollback.
Add Helm chart support to select LTS channel images/tags and expose release note URLs in chart annotations.
Define what qualifies as security patch for LTS, expected turnaround, comms path, and required verification steps.
Convert the working checklist into a formal release runbook with clear owners and time estimates.
Implement targeted scheduler smoke tests (queueing/backpressure/load-shedding) that commonly regress under backports.
Add signing/checksum generation and provenance metadata to LTS build artifacts; document verification steps for enterprise customers.
PRD covering customer requirements, packaging expectations (Hosted/Dedicated/Private), and success metrics (reduced incident-driven upgrades, fewer urgent escalations).
Comms plan for internal (Support/CS/Sales) and external (customers) distribution: cadence, templates, and what gets announced when.
Defines Console changes needed for LTS selection/pinning and how customers discover and consume LTS release notes.
Pilot execution ticket: select accounts, define success criteria, schedule patch cadence, and track issues/backport requests.
PR that introduces the initial LTS release branch, tagging conventions, and minimal config changes required to build/publish LTS artifacts.
